title: Time and viewpoint
summary: Use time anchors, event order and viewpoint to select tense and aspect and maintain a coherent timeline.

sections.title: Place events on a timeline
content: Compare ‘The team tested the alarm’ with ‘The team was testing the alarm when the lights failed.’ Both describe past time, but the second sentence views the testing as already in progress when a shorter event occurred.
Before choosing a verb form, underline every time expression and order the events. A tense name alone cannot tell you which viewpoint the sentence needs.

sections.title: Use Anchor, Order, View and Verify
content: Anchor: locate the reference time. Words such as yesterday, every Friday, since January, this week, when and by the time constrain the timeline.
Order: decide which event happens before, during or after another event. Past perfect can mark an event completed before a later past reference point.
View: decide whether the action is a habit or general fact, a completed event, an action in progress, or a past action with a result continuing to the present.

Verify: insert the option and reread the whole sentence or short passage. Tenses may change when the timeline changes; consistency means a coherent relationship, not forcing every verb into the same form.

sections.title: Let the timeline control the form
content: Consider: ‘By the time the caretaker arrived, the volunteers had moved the boxes.’ The arrival is the past reference point. Moving the boxes was complete before it, so had moved makes the order explicit.
Now compare: ‘The volunteers were moving the boxes when the caretaker arrived.’ Here the movement was in progress at the arrival point, so past continuous supplies a different viewpoint.
The forms are not interchangeable decorations. Choose the one supported by the stated time relationship, and avoid inventing an order that the sentence does not provide.

sections.title: Name the anchor and viewpoint
content: For two items, state the reference time, order the events and label the needed view before opening the options. Use the complete sentence—not one nearby word—as evidence.

sections.title: Control unfamiliar timelines
content: Apply the four checks without labels. Distinguish an earlier completed past event from an interrupted action, a repeated routine from a temporary current arrangement, and a finished past period from a period that still reaches the present.
Reject an option that is grammatical in isolation when it contradicts the time anchor or changes the event order.

sections.title: Name the earliest timeline failure
content: Anchor error: I missed or misread a time expression. Order error: I reversed which event happened first. Viewpoint error: I treated a habit, completed event, ongoing action or continuing result as the wrong kind of action. Sequence error: one choice made the surrounding timeline incoherent.
Do not repair tense by matching the nearest verb automatically. Redraw the timeline and explain the relationship that the corrected form expresses.

sections.title: Transfer the timeline method
content: Choose the form that makes one unseen past sequence explicit. A failed or hinted attempt enters a fresh parallel retry with different events and wording, so exposed recall is not treated as transfer.
